paper_title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Short-video search needs compact query rewriters that recover users' personalized intent from ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. Existing LLM-based methods have improved rewriting by using synthetic reasoning and subsequent consumption-behavioral feedback. However, overemphasizing subsequent consumption can favor engaging content over the user's immediate need, causing intent drift even when rewritten queries are grounded in behavioral history. We propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair uses human feedback according to how directly it reflects personalized intent, assigning feedback fidelity to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual queries and user reformulations from search sessions, and then screen them for contextual support. In the demonstration stage, a supervised fine-tuning curriculum progresses from large-scale context-to-query learning to reasoning and direct prediction on human reformulation and preservation. In the preference stage, direct preference optimization learns relative preferences from subsequent consumption feedback. In the verification stage, group relative policy optimization rewards exact agreement with reformulation or preservation targets to constrain intent drift. Further analysis shows that broad supervision benefits the full curriculum supervised training, while strict verification achieves better performance than auxiliary rewards. In offline experiments, WeFair-2B outperforms strong rewriting baselines in overall accuracy and intent preservation. An online A/B test shows relative increases of 2.593% in effective video-view rate and a 2.350% relative reduction in query reformulation rate. WeFair-2B has been deployed in the WeChat short-video search system, which serves over 100 million queries per day.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Personalized query rewriting is essential when an ambiguous search
query does not fully express the user’s immediate information need.
In short-video search, the intended meaning may depend on recent
searches, viewed content, or other context available when the query
is issued. Rewriting can expose this information to retrieval by
producing a more informative expression, but it must also satisfy
strict latency constraints [3, 4]. Therefore, the practical objective
is training a compact rewrite model that can resolve ambiguity
without replacing the user’s current intent and needs. Furthermore,
the rewrite pipeline also needs to accurately decide when to rewrite
or preserve the original query.
sections.content: Although general large-size large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, they fail to accurately understand diverse user intents and incur excessive per-inference latency, which is unacceptable for real-time search. To address these limitations, some approaches use synthetic Chain-of-Thought(CoT) traces to distill reasoning capabilities from large teacher LLMs into smaller rewrite models, and then use large-scale subsequent consumption feedback to align them with platform-specific user preferences. However, consumption-oriented alignment does not necessarily reflect the users immediate information need. When insufficiently constrained by direct evidence of user intent, rewriter may favor queries that retrieve engaging content while redirecting the original search intent, resulting in intent drift. Figure 1 shows an example of intent drift. To better capture personalized intent, recent methods incorporate actual user reformulations, which provide more direct evidence of how users clarify their information needs. PicQue[3] uses historical reformulations as context for generating training WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment for Personalized Query Rewriting Yingtao Ren et al. probability of rewrites associated with better personalized user intent. Finally, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) applies strict verification reward based on exact match with actual human reformulations or preservation. This final stage anchors policy updates to observed human expressions without adding graded similarity, retrieval, or other judge rewards. At inference time, the rewrite model directly outputs short rewrite or preservation decision, avoiding additional CoT generation latency. Figure 2 shows the overview of the proposed WeFair. Our further analysis suggests that the three training stages differ in their tolerance for supervision with varying intent fidelity. SFT can tolerate lower-fidelity supervision to acquire broad rewriting capabilities, while DPO can incorporate preferences inferred from subsequent consumption to refine candidate selection. In contrast, final GRPO optimization requires strict fidelity to the intended target. Auxiliary rewards may involve more fine-grained supervision but reduce rewriting accuracy. Offline and online experiments demonstrate WeFairs effectiveness in personalized rewriting. WeFair-2B rewrite model has been deployed in the online WeChat short-video search system, serving over 100 million queries per day. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We examine the role of supervision fidelity in personalized rewriting post-training. Demonstrate that extensive broad lowerfidelity supervision benefits curriculum SFT, while strict verification better supports on-policy alignment. (2) We propose WeFair, fidelity-aware framework that matches human feedback to demonstration, preference, and verification stages, enabling compact models to capture personalized needs while mitigating intent drift. (3) Offline and online experiments demonstrate that WeFair achieves strong rewriting performance with compact models and significant improvements in online WeChat short-video search.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
2.1 Personalized Query Rewriting
LLM-based query rewriting improves retrieval by enriching query
representations and adapting to search domains. Query2doc gen-
erates pseudo-documents, while CardRewriter incorporates plat-
form knowledge through knowledge cards [4, 22]. Domain adapta-
tion further aligns query expressions with retrieval requirements.
BEQUE combines supervised rewriting with retrieval feedback[17],
and negation-aware rewriting preserves explicit constraints [6].
MAAQR and QP-OneModel extend this direction through adap-
tive refinement and unified query understanding [8, 26]. Beyond
representation enrichment, IterQR and Think-Then-Rewrite incor-
porate reasoning into retrieval-oriented training[1, 11]. MiniELM
combines lightweight distillation with simulated feedback [14]. For
personalized search, user context and observed behavior provide
evidence of the user’s current information need, helping resolve
ambiguity and determine when to rewrite. PicQue combines hybrid
reasoning supervision with GRPO to address over-rewriting [3],
while Think-to-Personalize uses purchase history to support per-
sonalized retrieval [9]. WeWrite mines actual user reformulations
and trains with SFT and GRPO using lexical similarity and condi-
tional query-volume rewards [2].
sections.content: Figure 1: Overview of intent drift in WeChat short-video search. The original query crepe cake is redirected toward recipes instead of the intended eating videos. WeFair uses fidelity-aware human feedback through demonstration, preference, and verification to mitigate intent drift. examples that subsequently undergo manual verification, while WeWrite[2] directly uses mined reformulations for supervised finetuning and reward construction in GRPO. While these advances demonstrate the value of real user reformulations, the subsequent consumption feedback differs in how directly they reflect personalized intent, and its fine-grained use across training stages remains underexplored. To bridge the gap, we propose WeFair, fidelityaware alignment framework for training compact personalized query rewriter model in WeChat short-video search. Its central idea is to match supervision fidelity to the requirements of each training stage, improving how human feedback guides small model toward faithful and efficient rewriting. This progression can enable compact model to acquire personalized query rewriting capabilities while mitigating intent drift. WeFair combines automated data construction with three complementary training stages. We mine actual reformulations from search sessions and apply LLM screening and contextual verification to retain demonstrations grounded in user intent. Training then proceeds through three stages, each with distinct purpose. In the demonstration stage, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) curriculum progresses from context-to-query prediction to context-conditioned reasoning and finally direct query rewriting, building solid intent understanding capability. The broad coverage of human demonstrations prepares the compact policy model to generate useful candidates for later optimization. In the preference stage, direct preference optimization (DPO) learns from candidate pairs distinguished by subsequent consumption outcomes, increasing the WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment for Personalized Query Rewriting Yingtao Ren et al. Figure 2: WeFair training and serving. (a) Search sessions yield screened reformulation and preservation targets. (b) Progressive training aligns the model through demonstration, preference, and verification stages. (c) Rewrites expand the candidate pool through cache lookup and search while also informing online ranking. Furthermore, OneBar emphasizes content-grounded recommendations, while short-video and conversational query suggestion address consumption utility and intent coverage [13, 20, 21]. DVCQR aligns separate rewrites with sparse and dense retrieval [12]. These studies demonstrate the value of contextual and behavioral signals for query rewriting, while highlighting distinct objectives such as retrieval relevance, consumption utility, and personalized intent. On-policy optimization consequently requires considering the reliability of candidate-level feedback. TTRL shows that noisy pseudolabels can still yield reliable rewards [27]. This motivates prioritizing reward purity in on-policy preference alignment.

sections.title:
3 Methodology
Task Formulation. In the short-video search system, given a query
𝑞 and query-time user context 𝑐, a policy 𝜋𝜃 (𝑦 | 𝑥), where 𝑥 = (𝑐, 𝑞),
outputs a rewritten query ˆ𝑞 or a preservation marker ⊥. The ˆ𝑞
serves as an additional retrieval query, and the preservation marker
ensures that only the original query is retained. We define intent
drift as ˆ𝑞 changing or adding information supported by the 𝑐 but
differing from the user’s immediate needs. Define hallucination as
ˆ𝑞 introducing additional information unsupported by 𝑥. The objec-
tive is to generate context-supported ˆ𝑞 while preserving the actual
information needs.
Framework Overview. WeFair matches supervision fidelity to the
requirements of each training stage. We utilize context-to-query
records, user reformulations, and subsequent consumption feed-
back from search sessions. These signals capture a broad range of
user preferences but differ in how directly they reflect personal-
ization and immediate intent. Accordingly, curriculum SFT builds
rewriting capabilities from broad demonstrations, DPO learns rel-
ative preferences from consumption-grounded pairs, and GRPO
anchors final refinement through strict agreement with screened
reformulation and preservation targets.

3.1 Human Feedback Construction
We mine and screen search-session records to construct three super-
vision pools: a context-to-query pool C = {(𝑐, 𝑞)}, a reformulation
pool R = {(𝑐, 𝑞, 𝑞′)}, and a preservation pool P = {(𝑐, 𝑞, ⊥)}. All
used data are de-identified and sanitized to protect privacy.
Candidate mining. For context-to-query mining, we extract queries
𝑞 with their preceding context 𝑐 that have at least one effective
video view. An effective video view means watching a retrieved
video for more than ten seconds. We further screen all raw context-
to-query records with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, retaining queries that
are supported by the query-time context, yielding initial context-to-
query pool C0. For reformulation mining, we link eligible adjacent
queries to construct initial reformulation R0 within the same search
session, requiring no video click following 𝑞 and an effective video
view following 𝑞′. Each pair uses the context available when 𝑞 is is-
sued. Both records exclude suggestion-triggered queries and remove
system-generated suggestions from the extracted context. Since
adjacent queries still likely express different information needs,
candidate reformulations undergo rule-based filtering followed by
LLM screening for contextual support and intent continuity. Algo-
rithm 1 summarizes the construction process.
Rule-based filtering. After getting the initial candidates, we then
conduct rule-based filtering to R0. Let 𝑆 (𝑡) denote a string’s char-
acter set, 𝑎 = 𝑠 (𝑞), 𝑏 = 𝑠 (𝑞′), and 𝑈 = 𝑆 (𝑏) \ 𝑆 (𝑎), where 𝑠 removes
whitespace, non-word characters, and underscores. Thus, 𝑈 con-
tains the characters introduced by the reformulation. We filter a
candidate reformulation if any of the following conditions hold:
(1) No character gain: 𝑈 = ∅.
(2) Only gain function words: the added characters belong to a fixed

These rule-based filters remove uninformative changes and reformulations with weak lexical or contextual support, reducing noise in the candidate reformulation pool and limiting the workload of subsequent LLM screening. In our practice, about half of the initial candidate reformulations are filtered out at this stage. LLM screening. Intent continuity requires the reformulation to preserve the original subject, task, answer type, and essential constraints. Information gain requires useful retrieval information or meaningful entity recovery, excluding changes that merely alter formatting. At each stage, the models judge independently using the same input and screening criteria. This check determines whether contextual evidence supports linking the added detail to the current query. An isolated mention of the target query or broad historical interest alone is insufficient to justify the added detail. Each call returns acceptance or rejection decisions with brief reason, and malformed decisions are discarded. Details are provided in Appendix A. About one third of the candidates entering LLM screening pass both checks and form the final reformulation pool R. Refuse rewrite labels. We construct two types of preservation examples. Natural examples come from C0 where the original query 𝑞 leads to at least one effective video view, providing behavioral evidence that the query retrieves useful content. Hard examples come from reformulation candidates that pass the first LLM screening stage but are rejected during contextual bridging, as the proposed additions lack support in the query-time context. These examples teach the model to avoid unsupported personalization. We further use reasoning LLM to verify that the query is clear and that personalization cues are ambiguous. For verified examples of both types, we retain the original context and query and assign the preservation target, yielding the final preservation pool P. Finally, we remove the records selected for natural preservation from the initial context-to-query pool C0, and the remaining records form the final context-to-query pool C.

3.2 Fidelity-Aware Progressive Alignment
The training of WeFair follows demonstration, preference, and ver-
ification, with each stage initializing the next.
Demonstration: curriculum SFT. The curriculum consists of
three phases. Phase 1 trains the model to predict the query 𝑞 from
preceding context 𝑐. Phase 2 takes 𝑥 = (𝑐, 𝑞) as input and learns to
generate a teacher-provided rationale followed by the final target 𝑦∗.
Phase 3 predicts 𝑦∗ directly from 𝑥. Phase 1 uses context-to-query
pool C, while Phases 2 and 3 use a small part from reformulation
pool R and preservation pool P. C provides broad behavioral cov-
erage, while the smaller adaptation set teaches evidence-supported
rewriting, preservation, and the serving format. The rationales are
auxiliary explanations generated by Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview. For

required and preservation-required examples in the test set. During
the evaluation, all the evaluated rewriters use the original input
query and query-time context. We use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the
LLM judge, which additionally considers preceding and subsequent

For general LLM baselines, we evaluate DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Qwen3.8-27B. Furthermore, we reproduce two other adaptive rewrite methods, WeWrite and AWHCP, using the same training set. We reproduced WeWrite following the complete procedure described in its original paper [2], and adapted AWHCP [15] to the WeChat search system (Details in Appendix A). For our method, WeFair was evaluated at Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.5-2B, and Qwen3-4B. We mainly evaluate rewrite and decisionmaking quality of all baselines. Specifically, let 𝐶 be the count of judge-accepted rewrites on the rewrite-required set, 𝑊 be all triggered rewrites,𝑊𝑅 be the correct triggered rewrites decision, and 𝑃𝐶 be the correct preservations. Consistent Recall and Precision metrics are 𝐶/𝑁𝑅 and 𝐶/𝑊 , respectively. Exact match (EM) counts rewrites identical to the actual human subsequent reformulation, divided by 𝑁𝑅. On rewrite-required examples, Hallucination Rate counts triggered rewrites containing context-unsupported additions, whereas Intent Drift Rate counts context-supported rewrites that fail to match the users current information need. Both rates are divided by 𝑁𝑅. Rewrite-decision (RD) recall is 𝑊𝑅/𝑁𝑅, and preservation-decision (PD) recall is 𝑃𝐶 /𝑁𝑃 . Decision accuracy is (𝑊𝑅 + 𝑃𝐶 )/𝑁 , whereas overall accuracy is (𝐶 + 𝑃𝐶 )/𝑁 . All scores are percentages. More details about setting and implementation are shown in Appendix A

sections.title:
4.2 Overall Offline Performance
We present the offline performances in Table 1. WeFair achieves
the best overall performance. The WeFair-4B model reaches 73.48%
overall accuracy, exceeding the strongest large-size baselines Gem-
ini3.1 and DeepSeek4.1. WeFair-2B achieves 72.81% and the highest
consistent Recall of 83.95%. Its EM also exceeded the other two
adaptive rewrite baselines. Gemini 3.1 retained the highest EM and
the lowest Hallucination and Intent Drift Rates, while achieving
much lower rewrite recall. This suggests that large-size models
with CoT can substantially reduce hallucination and intent drift,
but yield more incorrect preservation. WeFair’s advantage lies in
the balance of successful rewriting and preservation. Notably, our
small-size WeFair-2B achieves significantly lower hallucination and
intent drift rates than other comparable rewriting methods (with
its intent drift rate reduced to about one-third), validating the ef-
fectiveness of our fidelity-aware training approach.
Intent fidelity. WeFair achieves lower hallucination and intent
drift rates than WeWrite and AWHCP, while more reliably preserv-
ing queries that did not require rewriting. Both baselines tended
to favor rewriting, particularly AWHCP. Even the smallest WeFair-
0.8B surpasses AWHCP-8B in preservation. The large-size LLMs
generally had lower intent drift rates than WeFair but also lower
successful-rewrite recall. These trends support the value of fidelity-
aware alignment with human feedback in mitigating intent drift
while maintaining effective personalized rewriting.
sections.content: Gains from model scaling. WeFairs overall accuracy increased by 5.91 percentage points from 0.8B to 2B, but only 0.67 points from 2B to 4B, while consistent recall remained nearly unchanged. These results indicate diminishing gains over the backbone sizes, with most of the observed gain already attained at 2B. Inference mode. Direct WeFair exceeds WeFair-CoT in overall accuracy at both 2B and 4B, and also achieves lower intent drift. CoT variants yield higher EM and PD Recall, but these gains did not translate into better overall performance, indicating explicit reasoning is unnecessary for the strongest results in these comparisons. For general large-size LLMs, we observe that Qwen3.8-27B with CoT achieves much better performance than direct prediction. These results suggest that our fidelity-aware training enables the rewriter to perform more effective implicit reasoning than explicit CoT. We further analyze the corresponding decode tokens and inference latency in Section 4.5.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.content: 4.3.1 Ablation Study of Curriculum SFT. To examine the role of curriculum learning in the SFT stage, we ablate the C2Q and CoT phases before direct human-target adaptation (HR). All four variants use the same number of human reformulation examples, but C2Q adds context-to-query samples in 𝐶. The results in Table 2 show that this broader, lower-fidelity demonstration supervision is most beneficial when combined with the subsequent humantarget learning phases. Specifically, C2QHR improves consistent recall over HR Only but reduces preservation recall, producing little overall gain. CoTHR achieves higher preservation recall and decision accuracy than both variants, supporting the contribution of reasoning supervision to rewrite-or-preserve decisions. These findings suggest that the broad and lower-fidelity C2Q and CoT supervision can aid capability acquisition in our curriculum SFT. 4.3.2 Ablation Study of Progressive Alignment. To assess the contribution of each stage in our progressive alignment framework, we compared four training configurations on the 2B model: SFT Only, SFTDPO, SFTGRPO, and the full training sequence (WeFair). All configurations use the same total amount of training data. Results are shown in Table 3. Demonstration builds the rewriting foundation. Our curriculum SFT already surpasses all evaluated adaptive baseline variants in consistent recall. This supports the effectiveness of demonstrationbased learning in establishing rewriting capabilities in compact models. However, its low PD recall reveals strong tendency to rewrite queries even when preservation is appropriate. Demonstration learning provides capable starting point but remains insufficient for reliable rewrite-or-preserve decisions. Consumption preference alignment further improves rewriting. The subsequent consumption-guided DPO yields modest improvements in consistent recall and precision, further strengthening successful rewriting. However, PD Recall decreases slightly, also indicating an increased tendency to rewrite preservation-required queries. This imbalance limits the improvement in overall accuracy, suggesting that consumption-based preference alignment refines rewriting capabilities but cannot reduce over-writing. Verification delivers the largest benefits. Adding strict-verification GRPO produces the largest improvement in overall accuracy, substantially improving preservation while maintaining high rewritedecision recall. Importantly, the full sequence achieves higher consistent recall and precision than SFTGRPO. These gaps even exceed the corresponding gains from adding DPO to SFT alone, suggesting that the value of preference alignment extends beyond its immediate improvements. Although SFTGRPO achieves slightly higher PD recall, the full sequence delivers the best overall performance by combining successful rewriting with effective preservation. All these ablation results support the complementary roles of demonstration, preference, and verification. Their progressive combination achieves the strongest overall performance.

SV reward pattern achieves the highest positive and overall advantage purity, together with the strongest overall accuracy among the evaluated configurations. Adding RM feedback reduces positive purity and substantially weakens preservation, suggesting that auxiliary reward models provide less reliable positive reinforcement than strict target agreement. SV has lower negative purity than RM-Augmented Verification, consistent with exact matching discouraging some acceptable alternative reformulations. However, according to the SV setting, whenever certain responses are assigned negative advantage, there always is perfectly matching response that provides positive reward. Consequently, the impact of incorrect negative advantage on the SV model is likely to be weakened. These results support prioritizing high-fidelity verification in final on-policy alignment without implying perfect semantic supervision. The RM-Augmented Verification 4 Vote variant improves overall accuracy over RM-Augmented Verification but lowers both positive and overall advantage purity. Four Vote setting over repeated judgments from the same RM therefore does not automatically make the induced advantage signals more reliable. This discrepancy also shows that advantage purity is diagnostic of training-signal reliability.

sections.content: when CoT is enabled. All the results are reported in Table 5. The details of the implementation are described in Appendix A. General-purpose LLMs achieve competitive rewriting performance without task-specific fine-tuning, but their full-CoT configurations incur substantial decoding overhead. The CoTDirect comparison for Qwen3.8-27B illustrates this trade-off. Explicit reasoning improves rewriting quality but sharply increases inference time, making full-CoT inference impractical in real-time search systems. In contrast, WeFair achieves low latency while retaining strong rewrite quality. WeFair-2B required only 7.60 decoded tokens and 0.316 per sample, compared with 26.65 tokens and 0.795 for WeFair-CoT-2B. At 4B size, direct WeFair used 72.66% fewer tokens and achieved 2.32 speedup over its CoT variant. Notably, both direct variants also attained higher offline overall accuracy than CoT variants(See Table 1). Relative to WeWrite at matched sizes, WeFair delivered higher overall accuracy and slightly lower mean latency. For the three direct WeFair variants, WeFair-2B retained nearly the latency of WeFair-0.8B while improving overall accuracy. Increasing the size to 4B significantly raises inference time with only slight accuracy gain. Accordingly, we select WeFair-2B for both online A/B testing and production deployment.

sections.title:
4.6 Online Evaluation
To evaluate WeFair’s online performance, we conducted a 10-day
online A/B test in WeChat short-video search, deploying WeFair-
2B on 16 NVIDIA L20 GPUs. The production control method is
WeWrite[2]. In production, WeFair generates rewrites for 42.26%
of processed queries and outputs preservation markers for 57.74%.
We measured click-through rate (CTR), effective video-view rate
(VV>10s), and query reformulation rate (QRR). We also measured
P95 model inference latency (81 ms) and the end-to-end search
latency increase (+16 ms). As shown in Table 7, WeFair with cache
+ vector retrieval strategy increases CTR and VV>10s by 2.951% and
2.593%, respectively, while reducing QRR by 2.350%. WeFair with
only cache retrieval also achieves improvement against the control
method. Additional lightweight vector retrieval further reduces
the query reformulation rate. All improvements were statistically

Higher engagement and fewer reformulations validate the practical value of WeFair for meeting users immediate information needs. Online cases analysis. Table 6 presents four cases from our online search system. The first illustrates context-guided spelling correction and the next two illustrate intent-aware expansion: adding explanatory and recruitment details brings retrieval results closer to the users current needs. In the degraded case, adding Education Bureau provides relevant information, but the rewrite omits XX City, which is needed to identify the intended account. The rewrite query therefore remains incomplete despite being topically relevant. Together with the online gains, these examples support WeFairs effectiveness in translating contextual clues into rewrites that better serve personalized information needs.

sections.title:
5 Conclusion
We presented WeFair, a fidelity-aware alignment framework for
training compact personalized query rewriters that mitigate intent
drift. The framework matches human feedback to three complemen-
tary roles: demonstration through curriculum SFT, preference learn-
ing through DPO, and verification through GRPO. Offline experi-
ments showed that WeFair achieves the best overall accuracy and
reduced intent drift while maintaining low inference latency. A 10-
day online A/B test further showed significant gains in engagement
and fewer query reformulations. Furthermore, our analyses revealed
that broad, lower-fidelity context-to-query supervision benefited
the complete SFT curriculum, while consumption-based preference
learning complemented subsequent verification. In GRPO, strict
agreement with human targets yielded higher overall accuracy than
the tested auxiliary rewards. These findings support matching su-
pervision fidelity to the role of each training stage. Our method has
been deployed in WeChat short-video search, demonstrating the
practical value of proposed fidelity-aware alignment for effective
personalization under production latency constraints.

Further Implementation Details A.1 Adaptation of AWHCP Our local adaptation retains AWHCPs ProblemIntentionFix Rewrite (PIFR) structure and SFTDPOGRPO sequence [15], while replacing its e-commerce data and feedback services with resources available for WeChat short-video search. Forward examples attach PIFR explanations to existing human reformulation targets, and backward examples are synthesized from real content titles. SFT mixes fast and slow responses without revealing the mode in the input. For DPO, each actor generates fast and slow candidates after shared problem description. The 2B experiment starts from Qwen3.5-2B, whereas the 8B experiment starts from Qwen3-8B. The main adaptations are feedback and optimization. frozen BM25 index of training-visible titles replaces the original productsearch service. Its relevance proxy combines lexical similarity to the query and preceding context, without access to the target reformulation. DPO preferences favor larger gains in newly retrieved relevant titles under this proxy. local Qwen3.8-27B teacher supplies weak labels for the quality judge, replacing the original combination of LLM labeling and expert review. Our output protocol explicitly distinguishes rewriting from preservation, while retaining the original reward weights of 0.3, 0.1, and 0.6 for quality, format, and retrieval increment. The retained DPO configuration uses learning rate of 107, 𝛽 = 0.5, and one epoch. GRPO uses batches of 128 queries with eight responses per query, learning rate of 106, and KL coefficient of 0.001. It allows 7680 input and 512 response tokens to accommodate user histories. These archived implementations therefore represent platform adaptation, with differences in supervision, retrieval feedback, and mode allocation. A.2 Training Settings During SFT training, we use AdamW with learning rate of 5106, weight decay of 0.01, and an effective batch size of 32 examples. For the DPO training, we continue from the SFT policy using preference pairs constructed from user reformulations and subsequent consumption feedback. Each pair shares the same original query and query-time context. For rewrite-required examples, human reformulations or consumption-supported candidates serve as preferred responses. The candidates whose observed retrieval results contain none of the relevant consumed items serve as negative responses. Preservation examples favor the preservation marker over generated rewrites. Missing feedback is excluded, and the subsequent consumption-based behavior feedback is used only to construct supervision. DPO thus learns relative preferences before final GRPO refinement returns to strict human-target verification. Because preference construction relies on sensitive search and consumption histories, we describe its principles while withholding raw user-level records and privacy-sensitive details of the internal feedback-processing pipeline. DPO uses learning rate of 106, 𝛽 = 0.5, and an effective batch size of 32 preference pairs. In GRPO training, this configuration uses DPO-trained model as its GRPO initial checkpoint. Table 8 provides the hyperparameter settings for the GRPO strict-verification training in WeFair. Advantages are centered within each response group without division by its standard deviation. Here, we provide the details and number of training samples used. The training data span four consecutive weeks of search logs. Table 9 reports the sizes of the three supervision pools. The common test set is collected from the immediately following three days and contains total of 𝑁 = 19696 examples, comprising 𝑁𝑅 = 12528 rewrite-required and 𝑁𝑃 = 7168 preservation-required examples. It follows the training-data filtering pipeline and undergoes additional human review. Screening models Setting. The Context-to-query screening and the final verification of selected preservation examples use DeepSeekV4-Flash. The query-to-query human reformulation screening uses three large-size reasoning models Gemini-3.5-Flash, DeepSeek-V4Flash, and GLM 5.2, while contextual bridging uses three opensource large-size reasoning models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.5397B-A17B, and GLM 5.2. Both screening stages use the same majority-voting strategy, in which three models independently assess the same input, and at least two must accept. A.5 Fidelity Errors Interpreting In order to better clarify the intent drift problem. We provide case(in Table 11) to illustrate why contextual support, intent alignment, and correct rewriting decision must be assessed separately. This example has the original input query crepe cake. Recent user searches and views history support an interest in eating videos, whereas older history contains lunch recipe tutorials. Adding eating videos resolves the current need. Adding how to make has contextual support but changes the task, illustrating intent drift despite topical relevance. dairy-free restriction introduces an additional requirement unsupported by the available context, defining as hallucination rewrite. Although an output can both add unsupported information and change the search goal, the reported metrics use distinct categories: unsupported additions contribute to hallucination, while intent drift is reserved for context-supported rewrites inconsistent with the current need. Therefore, the dairy-free recipe in the example contributes to hallucination rewrite even though it also redirects the task. Preserving the original query introduces neither error, but still fails the decision when rewriting is required. Low hallucination or intent drift alone therefore does not establish successful intent recovery. Conversely, faithful alternative expression can pass semantic evaluation while failing exact matching. These distinctions motivate evaluating rewrite success and preservation alongside fidelity errors, and interpreting strict verification as conservative training signal to align human needs.
